3.11 Equity Valuation III: Relative Valuation

Valuation with multiples

Section titled “Valuation with multiples”

The methods of 3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models and 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow estimate future cash flows directly. In practice, relative valuation is used more often: find a group of companies with similar businesses (comparable companies), compute the ratio of their price to earnings, revenue or book value (a multiple), and multiply the target company’s corresponding number by this multiple.

The most common multiple is the price-earnings ratio (P/E): price divided by earnings per share. Computed with the last 12 months of earnings it is the trailing P/E; with analysts’ forecast earnings for the next 12 months it is the forward P/E.

Relative valuation is simple and intuitive, and it reflects the market’s current price level directly. But it rests on two conditions: the comparable companies really are similar to the target in growth, risk and profitability, and the market prices the comparable companies reasonably. If a whole industry is overvalued, a value based on industry multiples is overvalued too.

Check C1
The target company has much more debt than its peers and grows more slowly. Valuing it at the peers' average P/E times its earnings per share is likely to give a value that is:
With more debt and slower growth, should the justified P/E be above or below the peers'?
Companies in the same industry can still differ a lot in growth and risk.
Think about each in turn: how does more debt affect the cost of equity? How does slower growth affect the P/E?

What the P/E ratio means

Section titled “What the P/E ratio means”

Multiples are not a method separate from DCF; they carry assumptions about growth and risk. From the Gordon model (Gordon growth model), next year’s dividend is D1=(1−b)E1D_1 = (1 - b)E_1D1​=(1−b)E1​, where bbb is the retention ratio:

P0E1=1−br−g\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1 - b}{r - g}E1​P0​​=r−g1−b​

So the forward P/E depends on three factors: the payout ratio, the cost of equity rrr and the growth rate ggg. Other things equal, faster growth and lower risk (lower rrr) mean a higher P/E. Growth in turn depends on the return on reinvestment (sustainable growth rate): Exercises Question 1 derives how the P/E depends on ROE.

The inverse of the P/E, E1P0\frac{E_1}{P_0}P0​E1​​, is the earnings yield.

Other multiples

Section titled “Other multiples”
  • EV/EBITDA: enterprise value (enterprise value) divided by EBITDA. The numerator includes equity and debt, and the denominator is profit before interest; both belong to all investors, so the ratio is unaffected by capital structure, and also by depreciation policy. It is often used to compare companies with different debt levels. But it ignores capital spending: a capital-intensive company has a high EBITDA, but much of it must go into replacing equipment.
  • Price-to-book ratio (P/B): price divided by book equity per share. It suits companies whose assets are mainly financial and carried close to market value, such as banks and insurers. How P/B relates to ROE and the cost of equity is in Exercises Question 2.
  • Price-to-sales ratio (P/S): market value of equity divided by revenue. It can be used for companies with negative or very unstable profit, but revenue is not profit, so it must be read together with margins (Exercises Question 3).

In any multiple, numerator and denominator must belong to the same investors: equity value (price, market value) goes with numbers that belong to shareholders (net income, book equity), and enterprise value goes with numbers that belong to all investors (EBITDA, EBIT; revenue is also commonly divided into enterprise value).

Check C3
Two companies have identical businesses and the same enterprise value; the one with more debt has a lower P/E. This shows that its stock is cheaper.
Think: the two businesses and enterprise values are the same, but do the shareholders bear the same risk? With different risk, would they pay the same price for each dollar of earnings?

Cyclical companies and CAPE

Section titled “Cyclical companies and CAPE”

The profits of cyclical companies such as steel, automobiles and semiconductors swing widely with the business cycle, while their prices reflect long-run value and move much less. Then the current P/E can mislead. Figure 4-1 uses a simplified example.

Check C4
In Figure 4-1, set the amplitude of the earnings cycle to 0.5. When is a cyclical company's P/E highest?
The price changes little, while earnings are highest at the peak. When the denominator of the P/E is largest, is the P/E high or low?
When earnings grow fastest, they are not necessarily at their lowest. When is the denominator of the P/E smallest?
Set the amplitude to 0.5 in the figure and see whether the P/E moves with the earnings cycle.

For the stock market as a whole, Shiller proposed replacing current earnings with the average inflation-adjusted earnings of the past 10 years; this is the cyclically adjusted P/E (CAPE), also called the Shiller P/E. In Shiller’s data, the CAPE of the S&P 500 has averaged about 17 since 1881 and reached a record of about 44 in December 1999; from late 2025 into 2026 it has been roughly between 39 and 41.

Research finds that when CAPE is high, the stock market’s average real return over the following 10 years tends to be low. But the relation is far from exact: CAPE can stay very high for years, and using it to time purchases and sales works poorly. Whether CAPE can be used to estimate long-run expected returns, and what to watch for, is in Exercises Question 4; 4.11 Capital Market Assumptions discusses estimating long-run expected returns more systematically.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Relative valuation multiplies the target’s earnings, revenue or book value by the multiple of comparable companies; this assumes the comparables really are similar and the market prices them reasonably.
  • Forward P/E P0E1=1−br−g\frac{P_0}{E_1} = \frac{1 - b}{r - g}E1​P0​​=r−g1−b​: it depends on the payout ratio, the cost of equity and the growth rate.
  • EV/EBITDA is unaffected by capital structure and depreciation policy but ignores capital spending; P/B suits banks and other financial companies; P/S must be read with margins. Numerator and denominator must belong to the same investors.
  • The current P/E of cyclical companies misleads; CAPE uses 10-year average real earnings and is negatively related to average returns over the next 10 years, but cannot be used to time the market precisely.
